beats.narration_text: A model passes its tests the day it ships. Eleven months later it is barely better than always guessing the same answer, and nobody changed a line of it. This is Sai. This week, a general one: MLOps, and the part of it that catches this. We will watch a real model go stale on real data, and find an alarm that does not need the right answers.

show.event: the ask types in under 'Hello, Sai'
the decay and the alarm land as result lines
the retraining line lands last and holds

props.segment: The Model Didn't Change. The World Did.
props.command: We shipped a model that tested well, and nobody has touched it since. Why would it be wrong a year later, and how would I know before the right answers come in?
props.runningText: freezing a model and waiting a year…
output: label-free alarm: KS on its own scores

beats.narration_text: First, the word. MLOps borrows its ops from DevOps. In Chip Huyen's guide, to operationalize something is to bring it into production: deploying it, monitoring it, maintaining it. The model is one piece. The rest is what keeps it right after launch: the pipelines that feed it, the answers that arrive late, the retraining. This video is about the middle word.

show.event: deploying · monitoring · maintaining fill the first row
pipelines, late labels and retraining complete the grid
the caption credits Huyen's guide

beats.narration_text: Here is a real one. Australia's electricity market, nineteen ninety-six to ninety-eight: every half hour, does the price go up or down? I trained a model on the first year and froze it. The next four weeks, eighty-four percent right. Then sixty-three. By week forty-eight, fifty-five; always guessing down scores fifty-four. Nobody changed a line.

show.event: always guessing DOWN in the same weeks: 0.544

props.title: One model, frozen after its first year
props.note: Recorded output, 2026-10-02: evidence/drift_run.py on ELEC2 (OpenML 151). Gradient boosting, seed 0, trained on weeks 0–51.

beats.narration_text: So what broke? Nothing in the model. The prices it saw after the freeze were not the prices it learned on. That is covariate shift. When the same prices start meaning something else, that is concept drift. Either can be caught without labels: compare this month's scores with training's, and take the biggest gap.

show.event: covariate shift typesets: P(X) moves
concept drift beneath it: P(Y|X) moves
the KS statistic: the largest gap between two curves

props.title: Two ways the world moves, one way to see it
props.note: Row 1, covariate shift: the inputs move. Row 2, concept drift: what they mean moves (after Huyen, 2022). Row 3, the KS statistic: s is the model's score P(UP), F its cumulative share.
props.conditions: D = 0: the same distribution; D = 1: no overlap. Here D rose from 0.14 to 0.81 and fell to 0.08 — no labels used (scipy ks_2samp, checked by hand).

beats.narration_text: In most products the right answer comes later, if at all. Here it arrives in thirty minutes, and just copying the last one averages eighty-six percent, ahead of both models in nineteen blocks of twenty. Most teams are not that lucky. So watch what you have today: the model's own scores. That gap rose as the accuracy fell, and fell as it came back, without a single label.

show.event: the question splits: wait for labels, or watch the scores
waiting works only when answers come fast
the resolver: the score gap tracked accuracy, r = −0.85

data.question: The right answers come later. What do you watch now?

branches.label: Wait for the labels
branches.fix: fine if they come in 30 min

resolver.label: Watch what you have today
resolver.detail: the score gap tracked accuracy over 20 blocks (r = −0.85) with no labels; labels confirm it later

data.ghostText: copying the last half-hour's answer scores 0.82–0.90 here: a 30-minute feedback loop

beats.narration_text: So retrain it? It helps, but it is not free. Refit every four weeks on the year before, the model never fell below sixty-two percent, against fifty-five frozen. But a year after the freeze, prices came back to where they started, and the frozen model came back with them, to eighty-five. Retraining had chased the strange year, and lost seven blocks of twenty.

show.event: one model trained on year one
it splits: refit every four weeks, or left frozen
the badges land — worst 0.623 and worst 0.548

beats.narration_text: So: one page. The model did not change; its world did, and later changed back. Accuracy needs the right answers, and they come late. The model's own scores do not: their shift tracked the decay. And retraining is a choice with a cost, not a reflex.

show.event: the artifact card opens on the decay
the price shift and the label-free alarm fill in
the retraining line closes it

props.artifactTitle: The Model Didn't Change. The World Did.
artifactLines: A model trained on a year of NSW electricity prices and then frozen scored 0.838 in its next four weeks and 0.548 by weeks 45–48, level with always guessing DOWN (0.544).
Nothing in it changed. The prices did: the KS gap between training and live prices rose from 0.22 to 0.92, then fell to 0.14 a year on, when the model recovered to 0.849.
With no labels, the KS gap on the model's own scores tracked accuracy across 20 blocks (r = −0.85). Copying the last half-hour's answer scored 0.82–0.90: labels here arrive in 30 minutes.
Retraining every four weeks beat the frozen model in 12 blocks and lost 7. Data: ELEC2 (Harries, 1999), OpenML 151; definitions after Chip Huyen.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you have a model in production, paste this. Ask which of its right answers you will not see for weeks, and what you can see today instead: the inputs, and the model's own scores against training. Then ask what you will do when they move: retrain, roll back, or wait for the world to come back.

show.event: the handoff prompt types in under 'Your turn.'
the label-free signals stack as it fills
the three choices land and the cursor holds

props.command: I have a model in production. Which of its right answers won't I see for weeks? List what I can monitor today without labels — the input distributions and the model's own scores against training — and for each alarm, tell me whether to retrain, roll back, or wait.
props.runningText: listing what can be seen before the labels…

beats.narration_text: The model didn't change. The world did. Sai.
